note: Practice questions (Claude-drafted, original wording) for B1 and B2, 300 per level, written to the CEFR scope of each level (grammar and vocabulary in line with the English Grammar Profile / English Vocabulary Profile level descriptions) with British and international contexts. Imported as drafts for teacher review.

passages.B1P_CYCLE: When Tom's car broke down for the third time in a month, he decided not to repair it. Instead, he bought a second-hand bike and started cycling the eight kilometres to his office in Leicester. The first week was hard: his legs hurt and he arrived at work hot and tired. But after a month he was enjoying the ride, and he had lost three kilos. He now saves about £150 a month on petrol and parking. The only thing he doesn't like is cycling in heavy rain, so on very wet days he takes the bus.
passages.B1P_REVIEWAPP: I downloaded 'StudyBuddy', a free app that helps students organise their revision. You enter your exam dates and subjects, and it creates a timetable for you. It also sends reminders and lets you test yourself with flashcards. I found it really useful, although the free version shows quite a lot of adverts. The paid version (£2.99 a month) removes them and adds progress reports. My only real complaint is that it sometimes crashes when you add a lot of subjects.
passages.B1P_NEIGHBOUR: Dear Mrs Jones, I'm writing about the tree in your garden next to my house. Over the last few years it has grown very tall, and it now blocks most of the light from my kitchen window. Some branches also hang over my fence, and their leaves fill my garden in autumn. I wonder if you would consider cutting it back a little. I would be happy to share the cost. Perhaps we could talk about it this weekend? Best wishes, Alan (number 14)
passages.B1P_SLEEP: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, but many people regularly get less. Scientists say that lack of sleep can affect our memory, our mood and even our immune system. Some simple habits can help: going to bed at the same time every night, avoiding coffee in the afternoon and keeping phones out of the bedroom. The blue light from screens can make it harder for the brain to prepare for sleep.
passages.B1P_MARKETHALL: The old market hall in the town centre, which closed five years ago, will reopen next spring as a food hall. More than twenty local businesses will sell food from around the world, and there will be space for live music at weekends. The council hopes the project will bring more visitors to the town centre, where many shops have closed recently. However, some residents are worried about noise late at night.
passages.B1P_INTERVIEWJOB: Last week I had my first job interview since leaving university. I prepared by reading about the company and practising answers with a friend. On the day, I arrived twenty minutes early, which gave me time to relax. The interview was more relaxed than I expected — they asked about my studies and a group project I had led. At the end they asked if I had any questions, and I asked about training opportunities. They phoned me two days later to offer me the job!
passages.B1P_ZERO: More and more people in the UK are trying to produce less waste. Some shops now let customers bring their own containers to buy rice, pasta and cleaning products, so there is no plastic packaging. Supporters say this can save money as well as help the environment, because you only buy the amount you need. Critics point out that these shops are still rare outside big cities, and that the products are sometimes more expensive.
passages.B1P_LANGUAGE: Many people believe that children learn languages more easily than adults. It is true that young children often develop a better accent. However, research shows that teenagers and adults can learn grammar and vocabulary faster, because they can use study strategies and understand rules. The most important thing, experts say, is not age but how much time you spend using the language and how motivated you are.
passages.B1P_HOLIDAYHOME: We rented a cottage in the Lake District for a week in October. The cottage itself was lovely — clean, warm and full of character — and the views over the lake were amazing. However, it was at the end of a long, narrow road, and the nearest shop was a 25-minute drive away, so we had to plan our meals carefully. It also rained for four of the seven days. Still, we would definitely go back, perhaps in summer.
passages.B1P_FESTIVAL: The Notting Hill Carnival takes place in west London every August bank holiday weekend. It started in the 1960s as a way for the Caribbean community to celebrate their culture. Today it is one of the largest street festivals in Europe, attracting around a million people. Visitors can enjoy steel bands, colourful costumes and Caribbean food. Because it is so crowded, the police advise visitors to arrange a meeting point in case they lose their friends.
passages.B1P_ROBOT: A hospital in Manchester has started using a small robot to deliver medicine and supplies between departments. The robot travels along the corridors on its own and can even use the lifts. Nurses say it saves them a lot of walking, so they can spend more time with patients. The hospital says the robot is not designed to replace staff, but to help them with simple, repetitive tasks.
passages.B1P_EXCHANGE: Last spring I spent three weeks in Lyon on a school exchange. I stayed with a French family, the Moreaus, whose daughter Chloé came to stay with us in the summer. At first I was nervous about speaking French, but the family were very patient. I went to school with Chloé every day, and in the evenings we often cooked together. The thing that surprised me most was how late they ate dinner — usually after eight o'clock!
passages.B1P_PODCAST: Welcome to this week's episode of 'Money Matters'. Today we're talking about student budgets. Our guest, Priya, managed to save £1,000 during her first year at university. Her tips? Cook in batches at the weekend, buy second-hand textbooks, and use a student railcard, which gives a third off most train fares. She also recommends checking your bank account every week, so there are no surprises.
passages.B1P_COMPLAINTREPLY: Dear Ms Clark, Thank you for your email about the delay to your order. I am very sorry that your sofa did not arrive on the date we promised. This was caused by a problem at our factory. Your sofa will now be delivered on Thursday 9th March between 8 am and 1 pm. As an apology, we will refund the £45 delivery charge. Please let us know if this date is not convenient. Yours sincerely, Mark Hill, Customer Services
passages.B1P_VOLCANO: Iceland has more than 30 active volcanoes. In 2010, the eruption of Eyjafjallajökull sent a huge cloud of ash into the sky, and much of the airspace over Europe was closed for six days. Around 100,000 flights were cancelled and millions of passengers were stuck. Although the eruption was not especially large, the wind carried the ash south-east towards the rest of Europe, which made the situation much worse.
passages.B1P_DIGITALDETOX: Last month I decided to have a 'digital detox' and use my phone for only one hour a day. The first few days were difficult: I kept reaching for my phone without thinking. But by the end of the first week I was sleeping better and reading more. I also realised how much time I had wasted scrolling through social media. I now use an app that blocks certain websites after 9 pm, and I leave my phone in the kitchen at night.
passages.B1P_THEATRE: The Globe Theatre in London is a reconstruction of the theatre where many of Shakespeare's plays were first performed. The original building burned down in 1613 during a performance of Henry VIII, when a cannon fired as part of the show set the roof alight. The modern Globe opened in 1997, close to the original site. Like the original, it has no roof over the centre, so some audience members stand in the open air.
passages.B1P_ADVICECOL: Q: My flatmate never does the washing-up and leaves the kitchen in a mess. I don't want to argue, but I'm getting really annoyed. What should I do? — A: Choose a calm moment, not when you are angry, and explain how you feel. Avoid blaming language like 'You never...'; instead say 'I feel stressed when the kitchen is messy.' Then suggest a simple rota so that you share the jobs fairly. Most people respond better to a clear plan than to criticism.
passages.B1P_PARKRUN: Parkrun is a free, weekly 5-kilometre run that takes place every Saturday morning in parks around the UK. It started in London in 2004 with just 13 runners. Today hundreds of thousands of people take part each week. You don't have to be fast — many people walk the course, and some bring their dogs or push buggies. Volunteers organise each event, and runners only need to register online once and print a barcode.
passages.B1P_WORKSHOP: Fix-It Café: Bring your broken things and learn to repair them! Every second Sunday of the month, 11 am – 3 pm, at St Mark's Church Hall. Our volunteers can help with clothes, small electrical items, bikes and furniture. Repairs are free, but donations are welcome. Please note: we can't repair mobile phones or anything that uses gas.
passages.B1P_CHARITY: Last year our office decided to raise money for a local children's hospital. We organised a bake sale every Friday, a sponsored walk along the coast and a quiz night in a nearby pub. In total we raised £4,200, which was twice our original target. The hospital used the money to buy toys and games for the children's ward. Several colleagues said the events also helped them get to know people from other departments.
passages.B1P_CITYBIKES: The city has introduced a bike-sharing scheme with 500 bikes at 40 stations. Users download an app, unlock a bike by scanning a code, and return it to any station. The first 30 minutes of each ride are free; after that it costs £1 for every extra half hour. The scheme has been popular with commuters, but some residents complain that bikes are sometimes left on the pavement.
passages.B2P_FASHION: Fast fashion — cheap clothing produced quickly to follow the latest trends — has transformed the way we shop. Clothes that once lasted for years are now worn a handful of times before being thrown away. The environmental cost is considerable: the textile industry uses vast amounts of water and produces a significant share of global carbon emissions. In response, some brands now offer repair services or buy back old items to resell. Critics argue, however, that such schemes are small compared with the overall volume of clothing produced, and that real change requires consumers to buy less.
passages.B2P_REMOTE: Since the pandemic, many employers have adopted hybrid working, with staff splitting their week between home and the office. Surveys suggest that most employees value the flexibility, citing the time saved on commuting. Managers, however, have raised concerns about the loss of informal learning that happens when junior staff can overhear and observe experienced colleagues. Some companies now require new employees to spend more days in the office during their first year, precisely to address this issue.
passages.B2P_BEES: Bees play a vital role in food production, pollinating around a third of the crops we eat. In recent decades, however, many bee populations have declined sharply. Scientists point to several causes, including the loss of wildflower habitats, the use of certain pesticides and the spread of diseases. Gardeners can help by planting a variety of flowers that bloom at different times of the year, so that bees have a source of food from spring to autumn.
passages.B2P_MUSEUMFREE: Most of the UK's national museums, such as the British Museum and the Natural History Museum, have been free to enter since 2001. Supporters of free entry argue that it makes culture accessible to everyone, regardless of income, and point out that visitor numbers rose substantially after charges were removed. Opponents counter that museums are struggling with rising costs and that overseas tourists, who make up a large proportion of visitors, could reasonably be asked to pay.
passages.B2P_CHESS: For centuries chess was seen as the ultimate test of human intelligence. That view changed in 1997, when IBM's computer Deep Blue defeated the world champion Garry Kasparov. Today, chess programs running on an ordinary phone can beat any human player. Paradoxically, though, chess has never been more popular. Online platforms allow millions of people to play against each other, and players use computers not as rivals but as training partners, analysing their games to discover mistakes.
passages.B2P_LETTER: Dear Editor, I was disappointed to read that the council intends to close the library on Park Street. For many residents, particularly older people and families without internet access at home, the library is far more than a place to borrow books. It offers free computer use, help with job applications and a warm, safe place to spend time. While I understand the need to save money, I would urge the council to consider alternatives, such as sharing the building with other community services. Yours faithfully, J. Patel
passages.B2P_SLEEPTEEN: Research into teenagers' sleep has led some experts to argue that school should start later. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts, making it natural for teenagers to fall asleep and wake up later than adults. A study of schools that delayed their start time by an hour found improvements in attendance and exam results. However, critics note practical difficulties: later finishes could clash with after-school jobs and sports, and parents who work standard hours might struggle with transport.
passages.B2P_FOODWASTE: In the UK, households throw away millions of tonnes of food every year, much of it still edible. Common reasons include buying too much, misunderstanding date labels and poor storage. A 'best before' date refers to quality, meaning food is often safe to eat afterwards, whereas a 'use by' date relates to safety and should be followed. Some supermarkets have begun removing 'best before' dates from fresh fruit and vegetables to encourage customers to judge food for themselves.
passages.B2P_ROUNDTHEWORLD: At 23, Laura Bingham cycled across South America without any money, relying entirely on the kindness of strangers for food and shelter. She described the journey as the hardest thing she had ever done, but also the most rewarding. 'I learned that people are overwhelmingly generous,' she later said. Her trip raised money for a charity supporting street children, and she has since completed several other expeditions, including a descent of the Essequibo River in Guyana.
passages.B2P_AI: Artificial intelligence tools that can write essays have caused alarm in schools and universities. Some institutions initially tried to ban them, but many have since accepted that such tools are here to stay. Instead, teachers are redesigning assignments: more work is done in class, oral presentations are being reintroduced, and students may be asked to explain how they reached their conclusions. Some educators argue that learning to use these tools critically is itself an important skill.
passages.B2P_HEALTHAPP: Fitness trackers that count steps and monitor sleep have become increasingly popular. Users often report that seeing their data motivates them to be more active. Yet researchers warn that the devices are not always accurate, particularly when measuring sleep, and that some users become anxious about their numbers. Doctors suggest treating the data as a general guide rather than a precise measurement, and focusing on long-term trends rather than daily scores.
passages.B2P_VOLUNTEERING: Volunteering is often presented as a selfless act, but research suggests it benefits volunteers too. Studies have linked regular volunteering with lower levels of stress and depression, especially among older people. Volunteering can also help younger people gain skills and experience that employers value. However, charities warn that volunteers need proper support and training; without it, they may feel undervalued and give up.
passages.B2P_HISTORYPUB: The pub has been at the heart of British social life for centuries, but its future is uncertain. Thousands have closed over the past two decades, due to rising costs, changing drinking habits and cheaper alcohol in supermarkets. Some pubs have survived by diversifying: offering food, hosting quiz nights, or even housing a post office or shop. In several villages, residents have bought their local pub collectively to prevent it from closing.
passages.B2P_SPACE: In recent years, private companies have become major players in space exploration, a field once dominated by governments. Reusable rockets have dramatically reduced the cost of launching satellites. Supporters say this competition will make space more accessible and drive innovation. Others worry about the growing amount of 'space junk' — old satellites and debris orbiting the Earth — which could collide with working satellites.
passages.B2P_CITYNATURE: Cities are often thought of as hostile to wildlife, yet some species thrive in urban environments. Foxes, for example, are common in many British cities, where they feed on food waste. Peregrine falcons nest on tall buildings, which resemble the cliffs they naturally use, and hunt pigeons. Urban planners are increasingly including green roofs, parks and wildlife corridors in new developments to support biodiversity.
passages.B2P_LEARNINSTR: Learning a musical instrument as an adult is entirely possible, despite the common belief that it must start in childhood. Adults may lack the time children have, but they often bring greater discipline and understanding. Teachers recommend short, regular practice sessions rather than occasional long ones, and setting realistic goals, such as learning a particular piece. Many adult learners say the greatest benefit is not perfection but the enjoyment and sense of achievement.
passages.B2P_TOURISM: Some popular destinations are struggling with 'overtourism'. In cities like Venice and Barcelona, residents complain that rising rents, crowded streets and short-term holiday lets have changed their neighbourhoods. Authorities have responded with measures such as tourist taxes, limits on cruise ships and restrictions on new holiday rentals. Critics of these measures argue that tourism brings jobs and income, and that the solution is better management rather than discouraging visitors.
passages.B2P_WORKWEEK: An increasing number of companies are experimenting with a four-day working week without reducing pay. Supporters argue that staff are more focused and productive when they have more time to rest. Trials have reported reduced stress and fewer sick days. However, the model may be harder to apply in sectors such as healthcare or retail, where services must be provided every day, and some managers fear that customers will be inconvenienced.
passages.B2P_CHOCOLATE: Chocolate has a long history. The ancient peoples of Central America drank a bitter drink made from cacao beans, often flavoured with chilli. When the Spanish brought cacao to Europe in the 16th century, sugar was added and it became fashionable among the wealthy. Solid chocolate bars only appeared in the 19th century, when new machinery made it possible to process cacao on a large scale. Today, most cacao is grown in West Africa, where concerns remain about low incomes for farmers.
passages.B2P_HOMEWORK: The value of homework, particularly for younger children, is hotly debated. Some studies have found little link between homework and achievement at primary school, while at secondary level the benefits appear clearer. Critics argue that excessive homework causes stress and reduces time for play, sport and family life. Many schools now favour short, focused tasks, such as reading or practising times tables, rather than lengthy assignments.
passages.B2P_ELECTRICCARS: Sales of electric cars have risen rapidly as prices fall and the number of charging points increases. Drivers praise the low running costs and quiet ride. However, many potential buyers remain hesitant, citing 'range anxiety' — the fear of running out of power before reaching a charger — as well as the higher purchase price compared with petrol cars. Experts expect these concerns to fade as battery technology improves.
passages.B2P_NOVELREVIEW: 'The Silent Harbour' is a gripping debut novel set in a fishing village on the Cornish coast. When a young woman disappears, the close-knit community is forced to confront long-buried secrets. The author creates a wonderfully atmospheric setting, and the main characters are convincingly drawn. If the ending feels slightly rushed, it is a minor flaw in an otherwise impressive book that will appeal to fans of literary crime fiction.
passages.B2P_LIBRARYSCIENCE: Researchers studying how people read on screens and on paper have found that, for longer and more complex texts, readers often understand and remember more when reading on paper. One explanation is that screens encourage skimming, as readers are used to scanning web pages quickly. However, the gap appears smaller among people who are trained to read carefully on screens, suggesting that habits matter as much as the medium itself.
passages.B2P_COMMUNITYGARDEN: Five years ago, an empty plot of land in east Manchester was full of rubbish. Today it is a thriving community garden where local residents grow vegetables, keep bees and run cooking classes for children. The project was started by a group of neighbours who persuaded the council to lease them the land for a nominal fee. Organisers say the garden has brought together people of different ages and backgrounds who previously rarely spoke to each other.

items.prompt: It's about time you ___ responsibility for your actions.

He is likely ___ the award.

items.explanation: Third conditional with 'have' as main verb: had had.

items.explanation: 'Under no circumstances' + inversion; the negative is already in the phrase.

items.prompt: The meeting, ___ was supposed to last an hour, went on all afternoon.

She is reported ___ two novels in prison.
